K-fold cross-validation randomly partitions the original dataset into $k$ equal-sized subsets, or "folds." The model is then trained $k$ times, each time using $k-1$ folds for training and the remaining single fold for validation. This process ensures that every data point is used for both training and testing exactly once. Finally, the performance metrics from each iteration are averaged to produce a single estimation of the model's predictive power.

In k-fold cross-validation, the original sample is randomly partitioned into k equal sized subsamples, often referred to as "folds" [p051]. Of these k subsamples, a single subsample is retained as the validation data for testing the model [p051]. The remaining k − 1 subsamples are used as training data [p051].

Under perfect multicollinearity, the independent variables are linearly dependent, causing the design matrix to be singular and its determinant to be zero. Consequently, the inverse of the matrix $X'X$ does not exist, which is required to compute the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) estimator. Without this inverse, there is no unique solution for the regression coefficients, making them impossible to estimate.

Under perfect multicollinearity, the design matrix has less than full rank because the predictive variables have an exact linear relationship [p069]. Consequently, the moment matrix cannot be inverted [p069]. This mathematical limitation means the system of equations has infinitely many solutions [p069]. Therefore, the parameter estimates of the regression are not well-defined [p069].

When faced with a group of highly correlated variables, the lasso tends to arbitrarily select just one variable from the group while shrinking the coefficients of the others to zero. In contrast, the elastic net encourages a grouping effect, where strongly correlated predictors are either included in or excluded from the model together. This behavior arises because the elastic net combines the $L_1$ penalty of the lasso with the $L_2$ penalty of ridge regression, which stabilizes the selection process. Consequently, the elastic net is generally preferred over the lasso when multicollinearity is present, as it provides more stable and interpretable models.

When dealing with a group of highly correlated variables, the LASSO tends to select only one variable from the group while ignoring the others [p015]. In contrast, the elastic net overcomes this limitation by adding a quadratic penalty term to the LASSO's penalty function [p016]. This modification allows the elastic net to handle groups of correlated variables more effectively than the standard LASSO approach [p015][p016].

The holdout method splits the dataset into a single training set and a single test set, whereas k-fold cross-validation partitions the data into k subsets and iteratively trains on k-1 folds while testing on the remaining one. This means holdout uses only one specific split for evaluation, which can lead to high variance depending on how the data is divided. In contrast, k-fold cross-validation averages performance across all k iterations, providing a more robust and reliable estimate of model generalization. Consequently, cross-validation makes better use of limited data compared to the simpler holdout approach.

For each iteration in k-fold cross-validation, one subsample is retained as validation data while the remaining k − 1 subsamples are used for training [p051]. Unlike the single run of the holdout method, typical cross-validation averages the results of multiple runs of model-testing together [p052].

This complexity arises because the algorithm typically involves solving a quadratic programming problem that requires computing and storing an $n \times n$ kernel matrix. While specific optimization algorithms like SMO can improve practical performance, the worst-case theoretical bound remains cubic in the number of samples.
